threats.name: Use After Free
threats.rationale: Use after free needs a manually freed or dangling reference. Swift manages class instances with automatic reference counting (ARC) and the library declares no class: every value is a struct or an Int and arrays are copy-on-write values, so nothing is ever freed while referenced. The residual routes are the Unsafe* pointer types, Unmanaged and C interop, which the library does not use. ARC is not a tracing collector; see the note on language-guarantee:swift-memory-safe-safe-subset.

NOTE: this rule does not exist today. Swift has no capability analyzer; LGE-A2 queues the swift .tokens and .grammar front end it needs, and wiring it into the report is LGE-W1.

No `class` or `actor` declaration, no file-scope or static `var`, no escaping or stored closure, no capture of self, no weak or unowned reference, no lazy property and no `nonisolated(unsafe)`: the only file-scope declarations are `let` constants of Int and String. Without shared mutable reference state a data race, a public mutable global and an ARC retain cycle cannot arise. NOTE: this rule does not exist today. Swift has no capability analyzer; LGE-A2 queues the swift .tokens and .grammar front end it needs, and wiring it into the report is LGE-W1.

In safe Swift every array access is bounds-checked, every variable is definitely initialised before use, nil is explicit in the type, and memory is reference-counted (ARC) with no manual free, so use-after-free, double free, out-of-bounds access and null dereference cannot corrupt memory without an unsafe construct. It holds only for builds that keep the checks: `-Ounchecked` removes the overflow and bounds preconditions (lane threat swift.ounchecked-consumer-build). ARC is reference counting, not a tracing collector, and the registry names its subset gc_runtimes; that an ARC runtime belongs to that subset is the analyzer rule's definition (flagged to the coordinator).

threats.name: Out-of-bounds Write
threats.rationale: Every array subscript in safe Swift is bounds-checked, so an out-of-range index traps (a crash, tracked as swift.runtime-trap-reachable-from-caller-input) instead of writes outside the buffer. The library's subscripts are all indexes derived from validated bits and from capped lengths (outputs[idx] in demux/decoder, Combinational.swift:250-251 and 299-302; sel[0], data[i], q[i] after count checks). The exclusion is CONDITIONAL on the consumer not building with -Ounchecked, which removes the bounds precondition and makes an out-of-range subscript undefined behaviour: the library cannot enforce that (swift.ounchecked-consumer-build). The exclusion therefore also requires the value-range rule (every index and size proven in range, so the exclusion does not rest on runtime bounds checks) and the no-shared-mutable-state rule (the library has only `let` globals). An excluded verdict holds for any build configuration only if the value-range rule is live; otherwise it holds for -O/-Onone only.

threats.name: NULL Pointer Dereference
threats.rationale: Swift has no null pointer: absence is an Optional that must be unwrapped. The only escape is a force unwrap (`!`), `try!` or an implicitly unwrapped optional, and the library has exactly two force unwraps: `sel.last!` (Combinational.swift:202) and `inputs.firstIndex(of: 1)!` (:353). Both are safe only by an invariant a few lines earlier (muxN's guards make sel.count equal log2(inputs.count) >= 1; encoder's guard makes exactly one input 1), and a refactor that breaks the invariant turns each into a crash. The one optional the library exposes is triState's `Int?` result (:445).

closed_by.detail: nil is expressible only in an Optional type. The library's one optional is triState's `Int?` RESULT (Combinational.swift:445), never a parameter; every other function takes and returns non-optional values. A force unwrap is the only escape, and that is the analyzer rule.

threats.name: Integer Overflow to Buffer Boundary
threats.rationale: The registry's CWE-190 is the narrow class where wraparound produces a wrong buffer size or offset; it says nothing about integer overflow in general (release text must render the full name, never 'integer overflow excluded'). Swift arithmetic traps on overflow instead of wrapping, and the library sizes its buffers with `1 << n` where n is capped at 16 before the shift (Combinational.swift:239-246, 288-295) and its sums are over validated bits (`acc + pair.element * (1 << pair.offset)`, :249-251, 299-301; `inputs.reduce(0, +)` :346; counter `q[i] + carry`, Sequential.swift:462-466). No wrapping operator (&+, &*) is used. Before PR #19955 `1 << n` was applied to an uncapped caller length; the cap is the fix.

threats.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
threats.rationale: The eleven gates are constant time and allocation-free on valid input (CMOS gate values are stack structs). The blocks allocate and loop in proportion to a caller length: decoder and demux build 2^n outputs with n <= maxSelectBits = 16, muxN and the encoders accept at most maxWidth = 65,536 lines, register at most 65,536 bits, counter at most 64, all checked BEFORE the allocation (Gates.swift:123-127; Combinational.swift:169-173, 239, 288, 337, 391; Sequential.swift:295, 444). Two functions have no cap on main: andN/orN loop over a caller array of any length (Gates.swift:599-608, 626-635) and shiftRegister over a caller state of any length (Sequential.swift:373-399); the work is linear in an array the caller already paid for, but nothing bounds it. threats.name: Reachable runtime trap (an uncatchable crash from caller input; also CWE-248 uncaught exception)
threats.rationale: A Swift trap (array index out of range, arithmetic overflow, force-unwrap of nil, `try!`, fatalError, precondition, allocation failure) terminates the process and cannot be caught with do/catch, so every trap reachable from caller input is a denial of service. The library has no try!, fatalError, precondition or assert; its traps could only be a subscript, an overflow, an allocation or the two force unwraps (Combinational.swift:202, 353). Before PR #19955 decoder/demux/muxN applied `1 << n` and `Array(repeating:count:)` to an uncapped caller length (a trap for n >= 62 or an allocation of terabytes); every size is now range-checked first and rejected with a thrown error. The remaining surface is reasoned, not proved: each subscript depends on an earlier guard. Not the same as -Ounchecked, where the checks vanish (swift.ounchecked-consumer-build). Swift's exclusivity-enforcement trap (overlapping access to one variable) is unreachable here: the library has no class, global var or closure state and no inout parameter.

closed_by.detail: No postfix `!` unwrap, `try!`, `as!`, implicitly unwrapped optional, fatalError, preconditionFailure, precondition, assert, assertionFailure or unreachable in the library. Run today it would flag Combinational.swift:202 (`sel.last!`) and :353 (`inputs.firstIndex(of: 1)!`), both safe only by an invariant established a few lines earlier. NOTE: this rule does not exist today. Swift has no capability analyzer; LGE-A2 queues the swift .tokens and .grammar front end it needs, and wiring it into the report is LGE-W1.

Value-range dataflow, not a syntactic rule (compare VER15a section 5.6): every + - * / % << >> and every subscript or Array(repeating:count:) size has operands proven in range from the validated domain (bits in {0,1}; counts capped by maxSelectBits, maxWidth, maxCounterWidth), so none can trap, none can overshift and none can allocate an unbounded amount; no wrapping operator (&+ &- &*). The shift rule must model Swift's smart shift: an overshift does NOT trap (`1 << 64` is 0) and a negative count shifts the other way. NOTE: this rule does not exist today. Swift has no capability analyzer; LGE-A2 queues the swift .tokens and .grammar front end it needs, and wiring it into the report is LGE-W1.

threats.name: Incorrect Bitwise Shift of Integer (Swift's smart shift)
threats.rationale: Swift's `<<` and `>>` are smart shifts: an overshift (`1 << 64`) gives 0 and a negative count shifts the other way, neither traps. A gate-block library is full of shifts: `1 << sel.count`, `1 << n`, `1 << pair.offset` (Combinational.swift:245, 250, 294, 300), `v >>= 1` (:33-36), `activeIndex >> bit` (:357, 408) and `n & (n - 1)` (Gates.swift:131). An unbounded count would silently yield an empty buffer and then a trapped subscript. Every shift count is bounded by the caps or a loop index.

threats.name: Numeric truncation before the call (caller converts a wider type to Int)
threats.rationale: A caller holding a UInt8, Int32, UInt64 or Double writes `Int(truncatingIfNeeded: x)`, `Int(x & 1)` or `Int(x)`; the conversion truncates or masks (4294967296 and 4294967297 can become 0 and 1; `Int(x & 1)` turns 256 into 0) before the library runs, and the library receives a valid-looking bit it cannot distinguish. (`Int(someDouble)` that is out of range traps in the CALLER, not here.) The compiler forces the caller to write the conversion, which is the only defence, and the contract comment says so (Gates.swift:110-113).

closed_by.detail: Every public gate takes Int (Gates.swift:193,235,280,323,368,403,438,478,506,533,562) and the n-ary gates [Int] (:599,626): Bool, Double (a `1.0` literal), Int8, UInt and String arguments do not compile because Swift has no implicit numeric conversion (a bare integer literal adapts to Int). Only an explicit conversion by the caller (`Int(x)`) yields an Int, after which the value is range-checked at run time. Nothing reads the signatures at report time.

Package-documentation claim (source-ref: a pointer to the stated contract, never a route and never live): every gate validates all of its own arguments left to right before computing, and Bool, Double and other integer widths do not compile, so the caller must convert explicitly (`Int(x)`).

threats.name: Unchecked error condition (the caller swallows the thrown LogicGateError)
threats.rationale: The error model is `throws`: a caller must write `try`, but `try?` turns an invalid bit into nil and `try!` into a crash. Swift-specific hazard: triState returns `Int?` where nil means high impedance (Combinational.swift:445-449), and `try? triState(data: d, enable: e)` also yields nil for an invalid input (Swift flattens the optionals), so a caller cannot tell 'disconnected' from 'rejected'. The package declares no @discardableResult, so ignoring a result is a compiler warning, but whether the caller handles the throw is the caller's program.

threats.name: Reliance on undefined behaviour under -Ounchecked (the consumer's build removes the checks)
threats.rationale: Built with `-Ounchecked`, Swift removes arithmetic-overflow checks and the preconditions behind array bounds checks, so a trap becomes undefined behaviour: an out-of-range subscript reads or writes foreign memory instead of crashing. The library's explicit `guard ... throw` statements are ordinary control flow and survive, so its input validation is unaffected, but every memory row of this file is conditional on the consumer not using the flag. The flag is the consumer's, not the package's (the manifest sets no unsafeFlags, Package.swift:21-43).

closed_by.detail: In safe Swift every array access is bounds-checked, every variable is definitely initialised before use, nil is explicit in the type, and memory is reference-counted (ARC) with no manual free, so use-after-free, double free, out-of-bounds access and null dereference cannot corrupt memory without an unsafe construct. It holds only for builds that keep the checks: `-Ounchecked` removes the overflow and bounds preconditions (lane threat swift.ounchecked-consumer-build). ARC is reference counting, not a tracing collector, and the registry names its subset gc_runtimes; that an ARC runtime belongs to that subset is the analyzer rule's definition (flagged to the coordinator).

threats.name: Memory leak through an ARC retain cycle
threats.rationale: ARC frees an object only when its count reaches zero, so two classes that reference each other, or a closure stored on an object that captures it strongly, leak for the life of the process, which a long-running caller feels as resource exhaustion. The library declares no class, stores no closure and its reduce closures do not escape (Gates.swift:606, 633; Combinational.swift:249, 299), so there is no cycle to form.

closed_by.detail: No `class` or `actor` declaration, no file-scope or static `var`, no escaping or stored closure, no capture of self, no weak or unowned reference, no lazy property and no `nonisolated(unsafe)`: the only file-scope declarations are `let` constants of Int and String. Without shared mutable reference state a data race, a public mutable global and an ARC retain cycle cannot arise. NOTE: this rule does not exist today. Swift has no capability analyzer; LGE-A2 queues the swift .tokens and .grammar front end it needs, and wiring it into the report is LGE-W1.
